title: A Blue Hour for the Inventory
premise: After his mother's funeral, Petra Pemberton returns to the shuttered family house and begins a written inventory of everything she never said — the locked room, the missing years, the man in the photographs who is not his father. When a late-night radio station plays an unrecorded song he recognizes from her humming, Petra traces it to Dez Okafor, the songwriter his mother loved and erased, now dying in a coastal town that remembers her differently than Petra does. As Dez's account collides with the inventory, Petra must decide whether loyalty to the dead means protecting their silences or breaking them open. He ends by forgiving both strangers — his mother and himself — recording the song at last, and letting the house, and its inventory, go.
about_author: Tamsin Vasquez is a former estate appraiser who spent a decade cataloguing other people's belongings before turning to fiction. She writes about inheritance, memory, and the objects we mistake for people, and lives near the coast with an unreliable record player.

chapters.title: The Inventory Begins
chapters.summary: Petra, POV. Three days after the funeral, he catalogs the house item by item, writing down what each object fails to say. The emotional beat is controlled grief curdling into suspicion when he finds a photograph of his mother laughing beside an unknown man, dated two years before Petra was born.

chapters.title: Item: A Locked Room
chapters.summary: Petra, POV. He pries open the room his mother kept locked all his life and finds sheet music, unsent letters, and a cassette labeled only with a date. The beat is trespass and thrill; the inventory method begins to fail him as the house stops behaving like property.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Petra, POV. Driving home through blue hour, a radio station plays a song he knows note for note from his mother's humming — one that exists on no album. The beat is vertigo; the past reaches into the present, and Petra turns the car around toward the station.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wrote It
chapters.summary: Petra, POV, shifting to Dez. At the station he learns the songwriter is Dez Okafor, once his mother's musical partner, now ill and living above a bait shop. Their first meeting is wary and electric; each recognizes the other as a keeper of the same silence.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers
chapters.summary: Dez, POV. Dez tells his version: the duo they were, the offer she refused, the night she vanished from his life without explanation. The beat is seduction of narrative — Petra wants to believe this stranger over his own memory, and feels disloyal for wanting it.

chapters.title: Contradictions
chapters.summary: Petra, POV. Back home, he cross-references Dez's story against letters and dates and finds gaps where the two accounts cannot both be true. Rising tension: someone has been in the house — pages of the inventory moved, the cassette gone. The beat is paranoia braided with doubt.

chapters.title: The Missing Tape
chapters.summary: Petra and Dez, alternating. They discover Dez's estranged daughter took the cassette, believing it proves her father was wronged out of royalties and credit. Confrontation forces Petra to defend a mother he no longer understands; the beat is loyalty and truth pulling visibly apart.

chapters.title: Side B
chapters.summary: Dez, POV. The tape surfaces: his mother's voice, young, singing the unrecorded songs, then speaking — confessing why she left, naming the fear and small betrayals that made her choose silence. The beat is devastation; Petra hears his mother become a full stranger, then a person.

chapters.title: Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Petra, POV. Climax. At the tide line outside Dez's window, Petra and Dez fight through blame to the truth neither wanted: she protected herself, imperfectly, and both men were collateral of her survival. Forgiveness arrives not as absolution but as accuracy. The beat is rupture becoming release.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Petra, POV. Resolution. In the emptied house, Petra records the songs properly, closes the inventory with a final entry forgiving the strangers in the photographs — including himself — and hands the keys to a new family. The last image is the radio playing the song, credited at last to both names.
